checkpoints.section: Why operating systems are prime targets
checkpoints.question: Why is a compromised operating system considered especially dangerous compared to a compromised application?

options.A: A compromised OS undermines security controls built above it since the OS is the foundational software layer that supports all other protections
options.B: A compromised OS prevents users from accessing files and forces a complete system reinstall before normal operation resumes
options.C: A compromised OS requires more patches than applications because it contains significantly more lines of code that need updating
options.D: A compromised OS allows attackers to bypass network firewalls completely and infiltrate other connected devices on the same network

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that a compromised OS undermines every security control built above it because the OS is the foundational layer on which all applications run. This makes it fundamentally different from a compromised application.

checkpoints.section: Patch Tuesday and the shrinking exploit window
checkpoints.question: What is the primary reason the window between patch release and working exploit code in the wild has shrunk to hours in some cases?

options.A: Organizations delay applying patches after release, which gives attackers sufficient time to develop reliable and functional exploit code
options.B: Vendors publish detailed technical documentation about vulnerabilities before or shortly after releasing patches to the public
options.C: Attackers reverse-engineer the patch itself to understand the underlying vulnerability that was fixed and develop working exploit code
options.D: Attackers now have access to automated tools that scan networks more efficiently and identify vulnerabilities faster than in the past

checkpoints.explanation: The section explains that once a patch ships, attackers reverse-engineer it to understand the underlying flaw because the patch itself describes what was broken.

checkpoints.question: What makes an end-of-life operating system a permanent security risk that cannot be remedied through vendor patching?

options.A: The operating system becomes incompatible with modern security tools and firewalls
options.B: The operating system loses the ability to connect to the internet and communicate with other systems
options.C: Users are unable to update their hardware to match the OS requirements
options.D: The vendor no longer provides security patches for any newly discovered vulnerabilities

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines an end-of-life OS as one the vendor no longer supports, meaning no more security patches are ever released, making every newly discovered vulnerability a permanent zero-day.

checkpoints.question: Why did the Print Spooler service represent a significant default configuration vulnerability on Windows systems?

options.A: It enabled anonymous users to access printer resources without authentication or authorization checks
options.B: It was exploited by PrintNightmare to allow both local privilege escalation and remote code execution
options.C: It required users to manually disable it before every system update to prevent exploits
options.D: It transmitted all print jobs in cleartext and exposed sensitive document data to network sniffing

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that the Print Spooler service was exploited by PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675 / CVE-2021-34527), which allowed both local privilege escalation and remote code execution.

checkpoints.question: What made Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) a critical privilege escalation vulnerability in Linux systems?

options.A: It allowed unprivileged local users to write to read-only files, including /etc/passwd, achieving full root access
options.B: It exploited a flaw in the sudo configuration that allowed standard users to execute root commands
options.C: It permitted privileged users to view encrypted files without knowing the correct decryption keys
options.D: It enabled attackers to bypass firewall rules and access kernel memory from remote network hosts

checkpoints.explanation: The section describes Dirty COW as a race condition in Linux's memory handling where any local unprivileged user could write to read-only files including /etc/passwd, achieving full root access.

checkpoints.question: How does a BYOVD attack bypass Secure Boot protections?

options.A: It modifies the UEFI firmware to disable Secure Boot before the operating system initializes
options.B: It installs a legitimately signed vulnerable driver that passes code-signing checks despite having a known exploit
options.C: It exploits a flaw in the TPM chip that prevents proper signature validation of drivers
options.D: It tricks the operating system into loading driver files from an untrusted network location

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that BYOVD uses a legitimately signed driver from a trusted certificate authority that Secure Boot cannot block, even though it has a known vulnerability.

checkpoints.question: Which type of privilege escalation moves a user from a limited account to an administrator or root account?

options.A: Horizontal escalation from one user account to another at the same privilege level
options.B: Sequential escalation through multiple intermediate privilege levels before reaching administrator
options.C: Lateral escalation by moving between different systems on the same network
options.D: Vertical escalation from a standard user account to administrator or root

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines vertical privilege escalation as moving from a user account to administrator/root, as illustrated in the table showing user to administrator/root transition.

checkpoints.question: What vulnerability does an unquoted service path create that allows privilege escalation on Windows?

options.A: Attackers can modify the registry entry for the service and change its executable path to point to their own malicious code instead
options.B: Non-admin users can read service configuration files and extract credentials that are stored in plaintext within those files
options.C: Windows tries to run executables at each space-delimited segment of the path, allowing a malicious binary at a guessable location to execute as SYSTEM
options.D: The service executable does not validate the digital signature of loaded DLL files before executing them during the boot process

checkpoints.explanation: The section explains that when a service executable path contains spaces and no quotes, Windows may try to run executables at each space-delimited segment, allowing a malicious binary at a guessable path to be executed as SYSTEM.

checkpoints.question: How does an SUID bit misconfiguration enable local privilege escalation on Linux systems?

options.A: It enables attackers to replace cron job scripts with malicious code that executes with root privileges
options.B: It permits any user to modify the sudoers file and grant themselves passwordless root access
options.C: It makes an executable run with the file owner's privileges, often root, instead of the caller's privileges
options.D: It allows the SUID binary to search for shared libraries in world-writable directories before system paths

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines SUID (Set User ID) as a permission bit that makes an executable run with the file owner's privileges (often root) instead of the caller's, and notes that unnecessary SUID binaries that can spawn shells are a classic escalation path.

checkpoints.question: What is the primary advantage of a bootkit infection compared to standard malware?

options.A: A bootkit disables the network adapter to prevent the system from connecting to security update servers and receiving patches
options.B: A bootkit prevents users from accessing the BIOS setup menu and changing boot device priorities to boot from external media
options.C: A bootkit can encrypt the entire hard drive without any user intervention or detection occurring during the encryption process
options.D: A bootkit executes before the OS loads and survives OS reinstallation because it resides in the boot partition rather than the OS

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that bootkits execute before the OS loads and survive OS reinstallation because they are installed in the Master Boot Record or EFI System Partition.
